pieces.title: A Small Fire in the Kitchen
pieces.author: Mara Vale
text: By the time the toast caught fire, we had been arguing for forty minutes about a chair. It belonged to neither of us. The previous tenant had left it beside the refrigerator with a folded newspaper on the seat, and for three years we had treated it as something that would eventually be collected.

I carried the pan to the sink. Outside, the man in the opposite building was watering his plants in a dressing gown. He moved from pot to pot without looking down at the street. I had seen him do this in winter, too, when there was nothing in the pots but sticks.
You opened the window and took the battery out of the alarm. Then you put the battery on the table, carefully, as though someone had asked you to demonstrate how a battery should be put on a table.
We ate the unburned slices standing up. There was marmalade left in the jar, but the knife could not reach it. You went into the other room and came back with a smaller spoon.

The chair was still between us. One leg had been repaired with a strip of green tape. I could not remember when the tape had appeared, or which of us had put it there. We had both started using the chair without noticing.

pieces.title: The Night Clerk
pieces.author: Elias Reed
text: At eleven the relief clerk arrived with a paper bag of oranges. He placed them in the drawer where we kept the spare keys and asked whether anyone had called for him. Nobody had, but he checked the message book anyway.

The hotel had nineteen rooms and a lift that stopped half a floor short of the third. Guests learned to climb out without being told. Once a month an engineer came to inspect it. He would leave his tools at reception and take the stairs.

That evening a woman in a wet coat asked for a room facing the station. She paid in cash and gave an address so close to the hotel that I could see the building through the glass doors. I copied it into the register.

She came down again just after midnight to borrow a pair of scissors. The clerk watched her go upstairs, then took an orange from the drawer. He peeled it in one piece and set the peel on the open register.

In the morning, the scissors were on the desk with a short length of blue thread wound around one handle. Her key was still missing. I went upstairs and knocked, but the room had already been cleaned.

pieces.title: Low Water
pieces.author: Ada North
text: When the reservoir fell, the old road came back. We went out on Sunday to see it, following the fence until the ground was firm enough to walk on. My father had brought a map, although he said he knew exactly where we were.

There were no houses. I had expected doorways, at least, or a chimney standing above the mud. Instead there were rectangular patches of stone and a concrete step with a rusted hinge at one end. Someone had placed a drinks can on it.
My father kept pointing toward a stand of trees on the far bank. The school had been there, he said. Then he unfolded the map and turned it around. My sister asked him where they used to buy milk.

We found the bridge at two. It was smaller than it looked in the photograph my grandmother kept above her television. The stream underneath was still running, carrying bits of white foam between the stones.

On the way back we passed a man with a metal detector. He showed us a handful of nails and a spoon with its bowl bent flat. He said he had found a wedding ring the previous week, but he could not show it to us because he had sold it.
My father folded the map along the wrong creases. In the car he asked whether we wanted to stop somewhere for lunch. Neither of us answered immediately, and he named the place we always went.

pieces.title: Room 6, Facing the Tracks
pieces.author: June Calder
text: The room had two lamps, but only one socket. To read in bed I had to unplug the refrigerator, which began to drip within an hour. I put a towel underneath it and read until the train came through at twelve seventeen.

Across the tracks there was a yard full of white vans. Each morning a man walked between them with a clipboard, opening the same three doors. On Thursday he brought a dog. The dog waited by the gate while he worked.

I was supposed to be looking for an apartment. There were four telephone numbers written on the back of an envelope, and by Friday I had called three of them. The fourth had been crossed out so heavily that I could no longer read it.
At the reception desk, the owner asked how much longer I would need the room. I said another week. He made a mark in his book and handed me a clean towel, still warm from the dryer.

That night I moved the refrigerator so I could reach behind the bedside table. There was a second socket, hidden by the headboard. I plugged in the lamp and lay down with my book. The refrigerator hummed beside me.
